events.title: Millet farming on the Yellow River
events.description: Villages at Jiahu and Peiligang grow millet, keep pigs and make some of the world's earliest playable flutes. Chinese civilisation starts on a river that floods.

events.title: Yangshao painted pottery
events.description: The Banpo village outside modern Xi'an leaves round houses, communal graves and red pottery painted with fish and human faces.

events.title: The jade city of Liangzhu
events.description: A walled settlement in the Yangtze delta builds vast water works and buries its elite with worked jade. Complex society in China is not only a northern story.

events.title: The Xia, half history and half legend
events.description: Traditional histories name the Xia as the first dynasty. The bronze-age site at Erlitou is the best candidate, but nothing found there yet says the name.

events.title: The Shang dynasty founded
events.description: The first Chinese dynasty attested in its own writing rules the middle Yellow River from a series of capitals, the last of them at Anyang.

events.title: Oracle bones at Anyang
events.description: Diviners scorch ox scapulae and turtle shells, then record the question and the answer beside the cracks. It is the earliest Chinese writing, and it is directly ancestral to the script still in use.

events.title: The bronze masks of Sanxingdui
events.description: A culture in Sichuan with no place in the traditional histories buries pits of gold, jade and enormous bronze heads with protruding eyes.

events.title: Battle of Muye ends the Shang
events.description: Zhou armies break the last Shang king, who burns himself in his palace. The victors write the losers up as drunkards and tyrants.

events.title: The Mandate of Heaven
events.description: The Zhou justify the conquest with a doctrine that will outlast them by three thousand years: heaven backs a just ruler and withdraws that backing from a bad one. It makes rebellion legitimate in principle.

events.title: The fengjian order
events.description: Kinsmen and allies are granted territories in return for military service. It works while the royal house is strong and dissolves into independent states when it is not.

events.title: The capital moves east to Luoyang
events.description: Nomadic raiders sack Haojing and kill King You. The court re-establishes itself downstream, and royal authority never recovers.

events.title: The Spring and Autumn Annals begin
events.description: The terse court chronicle of the state of Lu gives its name to two and a half centuries in which the great states swallow the small ones.

events.title: Duke Huan of Qi becomes hegemon
events.description: With the king reduced to a figurehead, the strongest ruler is acknowledged as protector of the Zhou order. It is the first of several such arrangements.

events.title: Confucius is born at Qufu
events.description: A minor official who never held real power spends his life arguing that government is a moral craft, ritual makes people humane, and the past is the syllabus.

events.title: The Art of War
events.description: The text attributed to Sun Tzu treats war as a problem in deception, logistics and knowing when not to fight. It is still on staff college reading lists.

events.title: The Warring States period opens
events.description: Seven large states fight for two and a half centuries with mass conscript armies, iron weapons and no pretence of Zhou authority.

events.title: Cast iron and the crossbow
events.description: China casts iron roughly seventeen centuries before Europe manages it, and fields a trigger-locked crossbow that lets a conscript outrange a trained archer.

events.title: Laozi and the Daoist current
events.description: The Tao Te Ching sets a counterweight to Confucian earnestness: govern less, yield rather than resist, and distrust the categories you are using.

events.title: Shang Yang's reforms in Qin
events.description: Rank by battlefield merit rather than birth, collective punishment, land made saleable, and the whole population registered. Qin becomes the most efficient and least pleasant state in China.

events.title: The Dujiangyan irrigation works
events.description: Li Bing splits the Min River without a dam, turning the Chengdu plain into the granary that will feed Qin's conquest. It still irrigates farmland today.

events.title: Qin extinguishes the last Zhou king
events.description: The dynasty that had been nominal for five hundred years is formally ended. Nobody outside Luoyang appears to have minded much.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang unifies China
events.description: The king of Qin defeats the last rival state and invents a title for himself: First Emperor. The unit of Chinese politics becomes the empire, and stays that way.

events.title: Script, coin and axle widths standardised
events.description: One writing system, one currency, one cart gauge so wheels fit the ruts. The empire is welded together by administration as much as by armies.

events.title: The northern walls are joined
events.description: Existing state walls are linked into a single frontier against the Xiongnu, at a cost in conscript lives that becomes proverbial.

events.title: Books burned, scholars buried
events.description: Histories of the defeated states and copies of the classics are destroyed to remove any standard against which the present might be judged. The story may be exaggerated; the intent was not.

events.title: The Terracotta Army
events.description: Some eight thousand individually modelled soldiers are buried to guard a dead emperor who had spent years hunting for an elixir of immortality.

events.title: The Dazexiang uprising
events.description: Conscripts who will be executed for arriving late decide they may as well rebel. Within three years the Qin, which was to last ten thousand generations, is gone.

events.title: Liu Bang founds the Han
events.description: A village official beats an aristocratic rival and takes the throne. The Han keep the Qin machinery and drop the worst of its cruelty, and Chinese people still call themselves Han.

events.title: Emperor Wu takes the throne
events.description: Fifty-four years of expansion in every direction, paid for by state monopolies on salt and iron and by taxing merchants nearly out of existence.

events.title: Zhang Qian is sent west
events.description: An envoy looking for allies against the Xiongnu is captured, escapes after a decade, and comes back with the first solid Chinese account of Central Asia.

events.title: Confucianism becomes state doctrine
events.description: The classics become the curriculum of officialdom. Government by examined scholars rather than by hereditary warriors starts here.

events.title: The Silk Road opens
events.description: Garrisons along the Gansu corridor make the overland route to the west safe enough for silk to travel one way and horses, glass and Buddhism the other.

events.title: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian
events.description: A court official castrated for defending a disgraced general finishes the history anyway, and sets the form every later Chinese dynastic history will follow.

events.title: Wang Mang usurps the throne
events.description: A regent takes the throne outright and attempts land nationalisation and currency reform. Both fail, the Yellow River changes course, and rebellion finishes him.

events.title: The Han restored at Luoyang
events.description: A distant relative of the imperial house rebuilds the dynasty from the eastern capital. The second Han is wealthier and less adventurous than the first.

events.title: Buddhism reaches the Han court
events.description: Monks arrive along the trade routes with texts that need translating and ideas that have no Chinese equivalent. It takes centuries to naturalise, and then it is everywhere.

events.title: Cai Lun's papermaking
events.description: Bark, hemp and old rags are pulped into a cheap writing surface. Everything about how China governs and remembers itself changes downstream of this.

events.title: Zhang Heng's seismoscope
events.description: A bronze vessel drops a ball from a dragon's mouth to indicate the direction of a distant earthquake, several days before the report arrives by road.

events.title: The Yellow Turban Rebellion
events.description: A Daoist healing movement turns into a mass rising against a court run by eunuchs. Suppressing it hands real power to regional generals.

events.title: Battle of Red Cliffs
events.description: A southern alliance burns Cao Cao's fleet on the Yangtze and stops him unifying the country. The romance written about it a millennium later is the best-known story in China.

events.title: The Han ends and three kingdoms divide
events.description: The last Han emperor abdicates. Wei, Shu and Wu spend sixty years fighting over the wreckage.

events.title: Shu Han falls to Wei
events.description: The smallest of the three kingdoms is taken from the north, and the balance that had held since Red Cliffs collapses.

events.title: The Jin briefly reunite China
events.description: One dynasty holds the whole country again for about twenty years, then tears itself apart in a war between eight princes.

events.title: The Disaster of Yongjia
events.description: Xiongnu forces sack Luoyang and carry off the emperor. Northern China passes out of Han Chinese control for over two centuries.

events.title: The court flees south to Jiankang
events.description: The refugee gentry re-found the dynasty on the Yangtze. The economic centre of China begins its long move south, and never moves back.

events.title: The Tuoba found the Northern Wei
events.description: A steppe people take the north, adopt Chinese administration, and eventually legislate their own language and dress out of existence.

events.title: Faxian sets out for India
events.description: A monk in his sixties walks across the Taklamakan to find a complete monastic rule, and comes home by sea fifteen years later with the texts.

events.title: The Yungang grottoes
events.description: Northern Wei rulers cut colossal Buddhas into a sandstone cliff, with faces that carry Gandharan and Central Asian features as much as Chinese ones.

events.title: Northern Wei moves to Luoyang
events.description: The court relocates south and orders Chinese dress, surnames and speech. It buys legitimacy and costs the dynasty its own army's loyalty.

events.title: The Sui dynasty founded
events.description: A northern general seizes the throne from his grandson and begins the reunification that the Tang will inherit.

events.title: Sui conquers Chen; China is one again
events.description: Three centuries of division end. The institutional repairs made in these thirty years underwrite the next three hundred.

events.title: The Grand Canal
events.description: Millions of conscripts link the Yellow and Yangtze rivers so southern rice can feed northern capitals. It works magnificently and it helps destroy the dynasty that built it.

events.title: The invasions of Goguryeo fail
events.description: Three enormous campaigns against Korea end in disaster. The cost in men and grain turns exhaustion into revolt.

events.title: The Sui collapse and the Tang are proclaimed
events.description: The second Sui emperor is strangled by his own guard. A garrison commander from Taiyuan takes the capital and founds a dynasty that lasts three centuries.

events.title: The Xuanwu Gate incident
events.description: Li Shimin kills two brothers at the palace gate and takes the throne from his father. As Emperor Taizong he becomes the model ruler of Chinese history.

events.title: Xuanzang leaves for India
events.description: A monk defies a travel ban and spends sixteen years crossing Central Asia and studying at Nalanda, then writes the geography up so precisely that archaeologists still use it.

events.title: Tang power reaches the Tarim Basin
events.description: Garrisons at Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar and Karashahr put the oasis cities under Chinese protection and the trade routes under Chinese tax.

events.title: Xuanzang returns with the sutras
events.description: Six hundred and fifty texts come back by camel, and a pagoda is built at Chang'an to house them while a state-funded team spends decades translating.

events.title: Wu Zetian declares herself emperor
events.description: A former concubine becomes the only woman to rule China in her own name, promotes officials on examination results, and is written up ferociously by the men who came after.

events.title: The Leshan Giant Buddha begun
events.description: A monk starts carving a seventy-one metre Buddha into a cliff at a dangerous river confluence, on the theory that the rubble alone will calm the water. It takes ninety years.

events.title: Li Bai and Du Fu
events.description: The two greatest Chinese poets are alive at the same time, briefly travel together, and write from opposite temperaments about the same collapsing world.

events.title: Battle of Talas
events.description: An Arab and Karluk force stops Tang expansion in Central Asia. Chinese prisoners are said to have carried papermaking west from here.

events.title: An Lushan rebels
events.description: A frontier general with three commands marches on the capital. Eight years of war leave the census down by tens of millions and the dynasty permanently weakened.

events.title: The twice-a-year tax
events.description: The equal-field system has collapsed, so the state stops taxing bodies and starts taxing land and wealth. Landholding is effectively legalised.

events.title: The great persecution of Buddhism
events.description: Forty thousand shrines are closed and a quarter of a million monks and nuns returned to lay life, largely to seize monastic land and metal. Chinese Buddhism never regains its institutional weight.

events.title: The Diamond Sutra is printed
events.description: A scroll from the Dunhuang caves carries the world's earliest dated printed book, six centuries before Gutenberg, and says so in its own colophon.

events.title: Huang Chao's rebellion
events.description: A failed examination candidate and salt smuggler leads a rising that sacks both capitals and massacres the foreign merchant community at Guangzhou.

events.title: The Tang fall and five dynasties follow
events.description: A warlord deposes the last Tang emperor. Half a century of short-lived regimes follows in the north and ten kingdoms in the south.

events.title: The Song founded at Kaifeng
events.description: A general is handed the throne by his own troops and then spends his reign making sure no general can ever do that again. Civil officials outrank soldiers from here on.

events.title: Gunpowder goes to war
events.description: Alchemists looking for an elixir of life produce an incendiary. Song armies field fire arrows, bombs and eventually the first true guns.

events.title: Bi Sheng invents movable type
events.description: Individual characters are cut in fired clay and set in an iron frame. With tens of thousands of characters to store, woodblock printing stays more practical in China.

events.title: Wang Anshi's New Policies
events.description: State loans to farmers, a hired militia, and government trading to break merchant cartels. The reforms split the bureaucracy into factions for a century.

events.title: The first government paper money
events.description: Sichuan merchant notes are taken over by the state. China runs a paper currency roughly six hundred years before anywhere in Europe tries it.

events.title: The Jingkang incident
events.description: Jurchen armies take Kaifeng and carry two emperors north as prisoners. It is the most humiliating date in the Chinese calendar and it is invoked for centuries.

events.title: The Southern Song capital at Lin'an
events.description: The rump dynasty settles at modern Hangzhou and becomes the richest, most urban and most commercial state in the world at that date.

events.title: Yue Fei is executed
events.description: The general who wanted to reconquer the north is killed on a fabricated charge by a court that wanted peace. He becomes the standard Chinese emblem of loyalty betrayed.

events.title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
events.description: A confederation on the northern steppe acquires a single leader and a discipline no settled army can match. Within seventy years it will hold all of China.

events.title: The Mongols destroy the Jin
events.description: The Jurchen state that had humbled the Song is annihilated, with Song help. The Song have removed their only buffer.

events.title: Kublai Khan proclaims the Yuan
events.description: The Mongol ruler takes a Chinese dynastic name and rules from a new capital on the site of modern Beijing. China is governed by a foreign house for the first time in its entirety.

events.title: Marco Polo at the Yuan court
events.description: A Venetian describes a country with paper money, coal fires and cities larger than anything in Europe. Readers assume he is lying.

events.title: Battle of Yamen ends the Song
events.description: The Song fleet is destroyed off the Pearl River delta and a minister jumps into the sea holding the seven-year-old emperor.

events.title: The invasions of Japan fail
events.description: A second seaborne assault on Kyushu is wrecked by a typhoon the Japanese name the divine wind. Yuan naval ambition dies with the fleet.

events.title: The Red Turban rebellions
events.description: Yellow River floods, forced canal labour and a millenarian Buddhist sect combine into a rising the Yuan cannot put down.

events.title: Ming armies take Dadu
events.description: The Mongol court withdraws to the steppe rather than fight for the capital, and continues to call itself the Yuan for another two centuries.

events.title: Zhu Yuanzhang founds the Ming
events.description: An orphaned peasant who spent years as a begging monk ends up emperor. He abolishes the chancellorship, purges tens of thousands, and runs the empire personally.

events.title: Zheng He's first treasure voyage
events.description: A Muslim eunuch admiral sails to India with over three hundred ships and perhaps twenty-eight thousand men, decades before the Portuguese round Africa.

events.title: The Forbidden City begun
events.description: A million workers spend fourteen years on nine hundred buildings. It is the seat of Chinese government for five centuries.

events.title: The capital moves to Beijing
events.description: The Yongle Emperor shifts the centre of gravity north to face the steppe, and commits the state permanently to feeding a capital that cannot feed itself.

events.title: The treasure fleets are ended
events.description: The voyages are stopped, the records suppressed and ocean-going shipbuilding restricted. China turns inward at the exact moment Europe turns outward.

events.title: The Tumu Crisis
events.description: A eunuch-led campaign loses an army and an emperor to the Mongols within a day's march of the Great Wall. The Ming go permanently on the defensive.

events.title: The Great Wall rebuilt in brick
events.description: The wall most visitors picture is Ming work: faced in brick and stone, garrisoned in depth, and built because the field army could no longer win in the open.

events.title: The Portuguese settle at Macau
events.description: A trading post at the mouth of the Pearl River becomes the first permanent European foothold in China, and holds it for four hundred and forty-two years.

events.title: Zhang Juzheng's reforms
events.description: The Single Whip reform consolidates a tangle of taxes and labour dues into one silver payment. It works, and it ties the empire's finances to imported American silver.

events.title: Matteo Ricci reaches China
events.description: A Jesuit learns the classics well enough to argue in them, and trades European clockwork, cartography and geometry for permission to stay.

events.title: Ming armies fight Japan in Korea
events.description: Two Japanese invasions of Korea are met by Ming intervention. Six years of war drain the treasury of the dynasty that wins.

events.title: Nurhaci founds the Later Jin
events.description: A Jurchen chief organises his people into banners, declares a state, and lists seven grievances against the Ming. His grandson will rule China.

events.title: Famine and rebellion in Shaanxi
events.description: Cold weather, failed harvests, unpaid soldiers and a silver shortage produce risings across the northwest that the Ming never suppress.

events.title: Li Zicheng takes Beijing
events.description: The rebel armies enter the capital and the last Ming emperor hangs himself on a hill behind the palace. He had reigned for seventeen increasingly impossible years.

events.title: The Manchus enter through Shanhai Pass
events.description: A Ming general opens the gate to the Qing rather than submit to the rebels. The Manchus take Beijing and stay for two hundred and sixty-eight years.

events.title: The queue order
events.description: Han men are given ten days to shave the front of the head and wear the Manchu braid, or lose the head. Resistance to it costs tens of thousands of lives.

events.title: Koxinga takes Taiwan from the Dutch
events.description: A Ming loyalist besieges Fort Zeelandia and turns the island into a base for a restoration that never comes.

events.title: The Qing annex Taiwan
events.description: The Kangxi Emperor takes the island, absorbs it into Fujian province, and then discourages migration to it for decades.

events.title: The Treaty of Nerchinsk
events.description: China's first treaty with a European power fixes the Amur frontier with Russia and is negotiated in Latin by Jesuit interpreters.

events.title: The Canton System
events.description: All Western trade is funnelled through licensed merchant houses at one city. It is orderly, lucrative and deeply resented by the people it excludes.

events.title: The Dzungar campaigns
events.description: Qing armies destroy the last steppe empire and settle the northwest. The territory becomes Xinjiang, the new frontier.

events.title: The Macartney embassy is rebuffed
events.description: A British mission asking for open trade is told that the empire possesses all things and has no use for foreign manufactures. Within fifty years the argument is settled by gunboat.

events.title: Lin Zexu destroys the opium at Humen
events.description: Twenty thousand chests of British opium are dissolved in seawater over three weeks. It is a legitimate act of drug enforcement and it is used as a pretext for war.

events.title: The Treaty of Nanking
events.description: Defeat in the First Opium War opens five ports, hands over Hong Kong and sets an indemnity. It is the first of what China calls the unequal treaties.

events.title: The Taiping Rebellion begins
events.description: A failed examination candidate who believes he is the younger brother of Jesus raises an army, takes Nanjing and holds it for eleven years. Twenty million or more die.

events.title: The Summer Palace is burned
events.description: British and French troops loot and destroy the imperial gardens in reprisal. The ruins are deliberately left standing as a national grievance.

events.title: The Self-Strengthening Movement
events.description: Arsenals, shipyards, a translation bureau and students sent abroad, on the theory that Chinese learning can be the substance and Western learning the tool.

events.title: War with Japan; Taiwan ceded
events.description: The modernised Japanese navy destroys the Beiyang fleet. Losing to a country China had regarded as a student is a greater shock than losing to Europe.

events.title: The Hundred Days' Reform
events.description: A young emperor issues over a hundred reform edicts in three months. His aunt places him under arrest and has six of the reformers executed.

events.title: The Boxer Uprising
events.description: An anti-foreign militia movement besieges the legations with court backing. An eight-nation force takes Beijing and imposes an indemnity payable until 1940.

events.title: The imperial examinations abolished
events.description: Thirteen centuries of recruitment by classical essay end at a stroke. An entire educated class loses its route into the state overnight.

events.title: The Wuchang Uprising
events.description: An accidental bomb explosion forces a garrison mutiny into the open. Province after province declares independence and the dynasty has no army willing to stop them.

events.title: The Republic of China is proclaimed
events.description: Sun Yat-sen is sworn in at Nanjing and hands the presidency to Yuan Shikai six weeks later in exchange for the emperor's abdication. Two millennia of dynastic rule end.

events.title: Japan's Twenty-One Demands
events.description: Tokyo presents terms that would reduce China to a protectorate. Yuan Shikai concedes most of them and destroys his own standing doing it.

events.title: The warlord era begins
events.description: Yuan Shikai dies after a failed attempt to make himself emperor, and the country splits among regional commanders for a decade.

events.title: The May Fourth Movement
events.description: Students protest the transfer of German concessions to Japan at Versailles. The demonstration turns into a wholesale attack on Confucian tradition and classical language.

events.title: The Communist Party is founded
events.description: Thirteen delegates meet in a Shanghai house and then finish the meeting on a lake boat to avoid the police.

events.title: The Northern Expedition
events.description: Nationalist and Communist forces march north from Guangzhou and break the warlords in two years.

events.title: The Shanghai massacre
events.description: Chiang Kai-shek turns on his Communist allies with the help of the city's gangs. The united front ends in a week and the civil war begins.

events.title: The Nanjing decade opens
events.description: The Nationalists set up a national government with a new capital, a central bank and genuine modernisation, on a base that never covers the whole country.

events.title: Japan seizes Manchuria
events.description: A staged explosion on a railway is used to justify occupying the northeast, which becomes the puppet state of Manchukuo.

events.title: The Long March
events.description: Encircled Communist forces break out and walk some nine thousand kilometres to Shaanxi. Most do not arrive, and Mao emerges from it as leader.

events.title: The Xi'an incident
events.description: Chiang Kai-shek is kidnapped by his own generals and released on condition he fight Japan rather than the Communists.

events.title: Full war with Japan
events.description: Fighting at the Marco Polo Bridge becomes total war. Shanghai falls after three months and Nanjing is subjected to a massacre of tens of thousands.

events.title: The capital moves to Chongqing
events.description: The government retreats up the Yangtze behind the gorges, taking universities and whole factories with it, and is bombed there for six years.

events.title: Japan surrenders
events.description: Eight years of war end with fourteen million Chinese dead or more. Taiwan is handed to the Republic after fifty years of Japanese rule.

events.title: Civil war resumes
events.description: American mediation fails. Within three years an apparently dominant Nationalist army has lost the north, its currency and its conscripts.

events.title: The Nationalists withdraw to Taiwan
events.description: The government, the gold reserve and the palace collection are shipped across the strait, and the Republic of China continues on an island of six million.

events.title: The People's Republic is proclaimed
events.description: Mao announces the new state from the Gate of Heavenly Peace. The civil war is effectively over and the strait is not crossed.

events.title: Land reform
events.description: Landlord holdings are redistributed to tenants in mass village trials. It is genuinely popular, and it kills something between one and two million people.

events.title: Chinese troops enter Korea
events.description: Volunteers cross the Yalu and push United Nations forces back from the Chinese border. The war ends near where it started, and the intervention is treated as proof China can no longer be pushed around.

events.title: The Seventeen Point Agreement on Tibet
events.description: Tibet is incorporated under an agreement its delegates sign under duress. Eight years later the arrangement collapses.

events.title: The Great Leap Forward
events.description: Communes, backyard steel furnaces and impossible grain quotas. It is intended to overtake Britain in fifteen years and instead causes the largest famine in recorded history.

events.title: Famine, and the Dalai Lama flees
events.description: Between fifteen and forty-five million die of hunger over three years while grain is exported. A rising in Lhasa is crushed and the Dalai Lama escapes to India.

events.title: China tests an atomic bomb
events.description: A device is detonated at Lop Nur, fifteen years after the founding of the state and two years after a border war with India.

events.title: The Cultural Revolution begins
events.description: Mao mobilises students against the party itself. Schools close, officials are beaten, temples and libraries are destroyed, and it runs for a decade.

events.title: The PRC takes China's seat at the UN
events.description: The General Assembly votes to recognise Beijing and expel Taipei. The Republic of China loses its international standing almost overnight.

events.title: Nixon visits Beijing
events.description: A week that ends twenty-three years of mutual non-recognition and splits the Communist bloc down the middle.

events.title: Mao dies and the Gang of Four fall
events.description: Within a month of his death his closest allies are arrested, and the Cultural Revolution is officially over.

events.title: Deng Xiaoping opens the economy
events.description: Household farming, foreign investment and price reform, all under one-party rule. Something like eight hundred million people leave poverty over the next forty years.

events.title: Shenzhen becomes a special economic zone
events.description: A fishing county opposite Hong Kong is designated an experiment in market rules, and grows into a city of seventeen million.

events.title: The one-child policy
events.description: Birth limits are imposed nationally and enforced with fines, sterilisation and abortion. They are relaxed in 2016, by which time the demographic damage is done.

events.title: Tiananmen Square
events.description: Seven weeks of student-led protest end when the army is sent into the centre of Beijing. The death toll has never been officially stated and the subject is unmentionable in China.

events.title: Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule
events.description: Britain hands back the territory under a promise of one country and two systems for fifty years.

events.title: China joins the World Trade Organization
events.description: Fifteen years of negotiation end with China inside the trading system. Global manufacturing reorganises itself around the decision.

events.title: The Beijing Olympics
events.description: A forty-billion-dollar opening statement that China has arrived, staged three months after an earthquake in Sichuan killed nearly ninety thousand people.

events.title: The Belt and Road Initiative
events.description: Infrastructure lending across Asia, Africa and Europe, framed as a revival of the Silk Road and read abroad as a bid for strategic reach.

events.title: Covid emerges in Wuhan
events.description: An outbreak in a city of eleven million becomes a pandemic. China holds a zero-tolerance line for nearly three years, then abandons it in weeks.
